claims.text: The initial tungsten-based refractory HEA intermediate layer is produced by spark plasma sintering and has a typical coarse-grained microstructure.
A single-step aging treatment at approximately 600°C can induce coherent nanoprecipitates in the tungsten-based HEA.
The nanoprecipitates induced by the proposed treatment will be uniformly distributed.
In situ monitoring can ensure uniform formation of coherent nanoprecipitates during aging.
The coherent nanoprecipitates effectively bridge microstructural regions.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces create enhanced pathways for phonon and electron transport.
The enhanced phonon and electron transport pathways increase effective thermal conductivity.
The coherent nanoprecipitates hinder dislocation motion.
Coherent nanoprecipitation can increase strength without compromising tensile ductility in a tungsten-based refractory HEA.
The aged layer will have significantly higher effective thermal conductivity than the untreated SPS-produced HEA layer.
The aged material will maintain or improve mechanical integrity at temperatures up to 800°C.
The beneficial thermal and mechanical effects will persist under cyclic thermal-mechanical loading up to 800°C.
Above 800°C, nanoprecipitate coarsening or phase instability may limit the beneficial effects.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says coherent nanoprecipitates preserve mechanical properties by hindering dislocation motion, whereas the cited abstract explicitly attributes strength-ductility compatibility to coherent interfaces facilitating dislocation transmission and relieving stress concentrations.

The predicted outcome permits mechanical integrity merely to be maintained, but the falsification rule requires a statistically significant improvement in mechanical performance. A sample with improved thermal conductivity and unchanged mechanical integrity would satisfy the prediction yet be declared falsifying.
